correctness.rationale: The normalized Example 5.3 equilibrium equations were reconstructed directly. At balanced mixing the positive equilibrium is \(I_1=I_2=(V-1)/(2(V+1))\); the Jacobian eigenvalues are \(-(V-1)(V+1)/(2V)\) and that quantity minus \(q\), so the local branch is analytic. Exact coefficient matching yields the displayed \(A\) and \(B\), and therefore \(\mathcal P''(0)\). Substitution into the source vector-prevalence formula yields \(\mathscr P''(0)=16Vq/(V^2+2Vq-1)^2\). The host numerator becomes \(y^3+2(1+q)y^2-4q\), whose derivative is positive for \(y>0\), giving the unique transition. The bundled checker verifies the exact coefficient identities and curvature identities symbolically and uses no finite enumeration as a proof.

originality.rationale: The source gives numerical contour evidence and qualitative language for the asymmetric-connectivity effect but no local curvature formula or exact transition. Related Ross-Macdonald work covers R0 rather than endemic prevalence, and related SIS work uses a different movement architecture. The result therefore supplies a new sharp local boundary rather than restating a known persistence or prevalence theorem.

value.rationale: The source identifies habitat connectivity and nonhomogeneous mixing as a difficult modeling question and relies on contour plots to describe the host/vector split. The exact second derivatives turn that observation into a sharp, interpretable local theorem: vector prevalence always rises to second order under imbalance, while host prevalence switches at a single explicit abundance–connectivity threshold. This directly explains why the source sees opposite host behavior at small versus large vector abundance and gives a reusable diagnostic for connectivity perturbations.
